title: ConFlux: Multivariate Time Series in Flux, One Unified Forecast in Confluence
claim: Many asynchronous, heterogeneous input streams should be merged through a structured mechanism into one unified output, like rivers flowing into a sea.
layout: 1 panel, left-to-right river flow, text labels overlaid on a landscape photo
description: A single full-width landscape image of an aerial river scene at sunset serves as a visual metaphor. On the left, several differently coloured streams (red, teal, yellow) run side by side. They are labelled 'Multivariate Time Series in Flux'. They flow toward a swirling whirlpool at the bottom centre, labelled 'Confluence'. A rocky headland in the middle carries the label 'ConFlux (Variate Sorting & Patching)'. From the whirlpool, one calm blue river runs to the right, labelled 'Unified Forecast'. It opens into a glowing golden sea at the top right, labelled 'The sea of Unified Prediction'. White handwritten-style text is overlaid on the photo. The eye goes first to the colourful turbulent water and the whirlpool.
caption: From flux to confluence: the core idea of ConFlux for
abstract: Real-world multivariate time series are inherently in flux: different variables evolve asynchronously and interact in complex, time-varying ways, yet accurate forecasting requires these dispersed signals to converge into a single unified prediction. This structural mismatch between dynamic, heterogeneous inputs and a unified forecasting objective poses a fundamental challenge for building general-purpose multivariate forecasting models, especially in zero-shot and large-scale settings. To this end, inspired by the idea that ``\emph{all rivers run into the sea}'', we propose \textbf{ConFlux}, a \emph{general-purpose foundation model for multivariate time-series forecasting} by learning to adaptively integrate cross-channel information under a unified forecasting objective. Specifically, ConFlux first reorders variables to reduce cross-variable entanglement, then aggregates adjacent variables into compact patches that can be processed by a Vision Transformer-style architecture. This design shortens the effective context, reduces attention complexity, and provides a unified token representation for pre-training and downstream tasks. Experiments on 25 public datasets show that ConFlux achieves state-of-the-art performance in zero-shot, fine-tuning, and from-scratch settings, while offering faster inference and lower memory usage.
